exchanges.question: How much of the roughly 500 basis point deceleration implied by the 9%-11% September revenue guide is supply constraint versus other factors like FX, and what are the supply constraints that are broadening beyond the advanced SoCs discussed last quarter? Follow-up: are Apple's reported efforts to seek greater memory sourcing flexibility about securing supply and mitigating memory inflation, or about preserving the customer value proposition?
exchanges.answer: Kevan: September total company revenue is expected to grow 9%-11% year-over-year, impacted by two factors: FX is a sequential headwind of about two and a half percentage points to the year-over-year growth rate from June to September, and the impact from supply constraints is expected to increase significantly sequentially, affecting iPhone, Mac and iPad; combining those two gets pretty close to the June total company growth rate. Tim: June constraints were primarily on Mac and to a lesser extent iPhone and iPad, driven by very high demand and the availability of the advanced nodes the SoCs are produced on, with less flexibility in the supply chain than normal; constraints are currently very significant with limited flexibility to remedy them. On memory: Apple paid more in the March quarter than December, significantly more in June than March (partially offset by carry-in inventory), and expects to pay even higher memory costs in September, partly offset by carry-in inventory (a benefit expected to decrease beyond September) and lower costs on certain non-memory components; beyond September, market memory pricing continues to increase, which could drive an increasing impact on the business. The DRAM market has primarily three suppliers; more suppliers would help on the supply side and perhaps pricing (unclear); Apple is evaluating all options.

exchanges.question: What adoption rates does Apple expect for the Apple Upgrade program across the two and a half billion device install base, and will it shorten the iPhone replacement cycle or equally benefit Mac and iPad, which have not had U.S. device subsidies? Follow-up: what are the learnings from the iOS 27 and Apple Intelligence public beta, will Siri AI be an iPhone demand driver this holiday, and how does beta usage inform compute costs and recovery of those costs through iCloud+?
exchanges.answer: Tim: Apple Upgrade makes it easier for customers to get the latest products with a leasing plan; residual values on Apple products are generally much higher than competitors, so it is a fairly affordable way in for customers who upgrade on a schedule; it is offered in Apple retail stores and not widely in all channels, uptake remains to be seen but early feedback is quite positive. Kevan: it is only available in the U.S. right now. On Siri AI: the developer beta was released immediately after the WWDC keynote and the public beta a few weeks ago, with overwhelmingly positive feedback from developers and reviewers; Tim called private, personal-context, OS-integrated AI a very big idea. On compute cost it is early going and Apple does not have a complete plan; it expects some people to use it a lot and will have upgrade possibilities on iCloud+ so users can buy up the stack. No adoption rate, replacement cycle or holiday demand figures were given.

exchanges.question: The Street had 12% September growth and the 9%-11% guide could be explained by FX alone; with the Street at 8%-9% for December, how much do the supply constraints hit the December quarter? Follow-up: could Apple broaden its silicon providers (e.g. the other company building a fab in Arizona) in a reasonable time frame to alleviate the constraints?
exchanges.answer: Tim: the primary supply constraint is the advanced nodes the SoCs run on; the root cause is a demand forecast issue rather than a regular supply issue, with iPhone up 22% (and 22% year-to-date) and Mac up 29% doing remarkably better than Apple's already high expectations; the supply chain has less flexibility than normal, Apple has been pulling supply ahead and there is a limit, so the September quarter will be one of scrambling on the supply side. Kevan: those dynamics plus the sequential FX impact are what is built into the 9%-11% September guidance; Apple is not providing any color or guidance beyond the September quarter, including December. On broadening silicon suppliers, Tim stressed it is not a partner or supplier issue but an incredibly strong iPhone and Mac product cycle with demand beyond expectation; Apple sources over 100 million components this year out of Arizona as part of its $600 billion U.S. commitment and could not be more pleased with how that fab has ramped.

exchanges.question: On the unprecedented price increases: does Apple intend to pursue multi-year LTAs with suppliers to lock in supply at pre-agreed prices, and in pricing is the intention to protect product gross profit dollars or product gross margins? Follow-up: 12% services growth was a bit below guidance and the fiscal Q4 guide implies below 10% reported growth; what factors drive the deceleration, and is App Store softness a function of AI reprioritizing time away from the App Store?
exchanges.answer: Tim: Apple reluctantly raised prices because it is in a 100-year flood on memory pricing with exponential increases; its philosophy looks at units, revenue and margin together and makes a business judgment over the long term rather than a 90-day clock, not a mathematical formula on one dimension; the multi-year LTA question was not addressed. Kevan: services growth went from 16% in fiscal Q2 to 12% in June, with FX the main driver sequentially, plus the year-ago theatrical release of F1 (which benefited the June and September quarters a year ago), App Store headwinds in mobile gaming, App Store business model changes in certain countries, and the U.S. court ruling on link-out transactions (the Supreme Court will hear Apple's appeal); the App Store still set a June quarter record, cloud services, video, payment services and advertising grew strong double digits, and Apple roughly met its expectations for the quarter with a bit more softness in mobile gaming. For September, FX is a theme hitting services more than the total company: about a 5 percentage point headwind to the year-over-year services growth rate from the March to the September quarter, with another two and a half point sequential headwind versus the 12% reported in June.

exchanges.question: Given the memory pricing dynamic, has Apple seen any pull-forward of demand from consumers, enterprise or education, and is that factored into its forward views? Follow-up: as AI proliferates to the edge, does Apple see additional addressable markets evolving from AI over time?
exchanges.answer: Tim: iPhone has been running at a 22% growth rate for the last while and 22% year-to-date this cycle, and pull-forward is not obvious in the data. Apple has now had to increase prices on iPad and Mac, and it is too early to reach a definitive conclusion on price elasticity because channel inventory takes a while to adjust and consumers take a while to respond; Apple will understand more in the weeks ahead. On AI, there are enormous opportunities for Apple, he is excited about Siri AI, and the ability to run some percentage of requests on device is very strategic and a competitive weapon; no specific new addressable markets were named.

exchanges.question: Will Siri AI change Apple's capital intensity, given that some requests go to the back end in both first-party and third-party cloud despite on-device and distributed compute? Follow-up to John Ternus: how is the competitive landscape changing, including potential AI-enabled devices from OpenAI or a SpaceX AI phone bypassing carriers, and where does Apple stand?
exchanges.answer: Tim: Apple uses a hybrid model with some third-party cloud and its own data centers, and there will be a mix; OpEx has been growing with quite a bit more spending on AI, and AI expenditures also sit in other P&L lines such as COGS; Apple will see what Siri AI does on the cost side, heavy users can move up on an iCloud plan, and the balance of those is a bit uncertain at the moment. John Ternus: reiterated there is so much opportunity in everything happening in the space; Apple is really focused on its own plans and very excited; no comment on specific competitors.

exchanges.question: What is the updated status of launching Siri AI in China and Europe, which were excluded from the initial rollout announced at WWDC, and what hurdles remain? Follow-up: gross margin was 48% ex tariff refund in June and the guide is about 46.5% ex refund; how much of the sequential decline is FX versus increased commodity costs?
exchanges.answer: Tim: in the EU Apple is working closely with the commission; its desire is to launch everything everywhere at the same time but it has not been able to in the EU, Siri AI is or will be offered for Mac there because Mac is not covered by the same regulations as iPhone and iPad, and Apple hopes to reach some solution. In China, last week Apple received approval to ship the original Apple Intelligence features such as cleanup, is working through that rollout, and more work is required down the road for Siri AI. Kevan: total company gross margin went from 49.3% in the March quarter to 48.1% in June adjusted for the tariff refund, a 120 basis point change of which more than 100% is explained by the memory cost change, with FX a factor but not the main driver and partial offsets from carry-in inventory, lower non-memory component costs and favorable mix; the move from 48.1% to the 46.5% September midpoint ex refund, a 160 basis point change, is also more than explained by memory cost with the same partial offsets, and FX is a pretty minimal impact versus memory.
